Chapter 1: Questioning the Roots of Morality and Truth
Ever get that subtle feeling something about the rules everyone follows just doesn’t quite add up? Picture yourself in a bustling café, watching people go about their day. Most seem pretty sure about what’s right and wrong—and there’s a certain comfort in that kind of certainty, isn’t there? But maybe, somewhere in the back of your mind, there’s a quiet, persistent question: what if these beliefs aren’t as rock-solid as they seem?
From the time we’re kids, we’re surrounded by ideas of good and evil, right and wrong. It almost feels like these are facts, as obvious as the sky is blue. But if you look a little closer, you’ll see that what we call “truth” is actually stitched together from centuries of habits, traditions, and unspoken deals. Even the world’s greatest thinkers—those philosophers we read about—weren’t just uncovering some universal truth. A lot of the time, they were shaping the world based on their own backgrounds, needs, and desires.
So, what if the philosopher isn’t some distant, neutral observer? Imagine instead that every philosopher brings their own history, personality, and instincts to the table. No matter how hard anyone tries, the search for truth is never completely separate from personal hopes and fears. Even those big, celebrated moral theories? They’re colored by the philosopher’s own story and hidden motives.
Picture a classroom on a quiet afternoon. A teacher is explaining to a group of students the difference between what is—and what ought to be. Most students are busy writing notes, nodding along. But then there’s that one student who asks: who gets to decide what “ought to be?” Why should anyone accept these rules without a second thought? The teacher, maybe without even realizing it, is passing on a tradition that goes back for generations—a tradition that claims to know what’s good, what’s evil, and what’s really true.
But here’s something to consider: what if these traditions aren’t the product of pure reason, but of instinct? What if our moral rules aren’t universal truths, but the result of long adaptation and the needs of those in charge? That one student’s quiet doubt grows into a restless curiosity. Suddenly, it’s clear—the search for truth isn’t just about finding hidden facts. It’s about questioning the very foundations those facts are built on.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our beliefs are shaped by the culture around us. The words we use, the stories we tell, the values we hold—they’re all tied to a specific time and place. Even philosophers get caught up in this web. That dream of pure objectivity—seeing the world exactly as it is, with zero bias? It’s just that—a dream.
